title: Closure, interior and boundary
objectives: Find the closure, interior and boundary of a set.

screens.title: Where small balls meet the set
screens.prose: The set $A$ is the open unit disc (dashed rim), the segment from $(1, 0)$ to $(2, 0)$ and the point $(0, 1.5)$. Move the probe ball with the sliders and shrink it.
screens.question: Tap every labelled point where every ball round it, however small, meets $A$.

hints.text: Points of $A$ itself qualify: the ball holds the point.
$(0.6, 0.8)$ is on the dashed rim, outside $A$.
Six qualify. Only $(2.5, 0)$ and $(0, 1.2)$ have a small ball missing $A$.

feedback.correct: Right. These six are the closure points.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Put the probe on each point and shrink it.

byKey.cir: You missed $(0.6, 0.8)$. It is not in $A$, but every ball round it reaches into the disc.
byKey.out: $(2.5, 0)$ is 0.5 from the segment. A ball of radius 0.4 misses $A$.
byKey.mid: $(0, 1.2)$ is 0.2 from the disc and 0.3 from the point. A ball of radius 0.1 misses both.
byKey.top15: You missed $(0, 1.5)$. It belongs to $A$, so every ball round it meets $A$.

explain.text: A point is a **closure point** of $A$ when every ball round it meets $A$. Points of $A$ qualify, and so does the rim. The closure $\overline{A}$ is the closed disc, the segment and the point $(0, 1.5)$.

screens.title: Inside and on the edge
screens.prose: An **interior point** of $A$ has some ball inside $A$; they form $A^\circ$. A **boundary point** has every ball meeting both $A$ and $A^c$; they form $\partial A = \overline{A} \setminus A^\circ$.
screens.question: Tap every boundary point among the six closure points.

hints.text: Remove the interior points from the closure.
A small ball round $(1.5, 0)$ leaves the segment.
Only the centre has a ball inside $A$. The other five are boundary points.

feedback.correct: Right. The whole segment and the lone point are boundary.
feedback.generic: Not quite. A boundary point has no ball inside $A$.

byKey.c0: The centre has the ball $B(0, 0.5)$ inside $A$. It is interior, not boundary.
byKey.s15: You missed $(1.5, 0)$. A segment has no area, so every ball round it leaves $A$.

explain.text: $A^\circ$ is the open disc. $\partial A = \overline{A} \setminus A^\circ$ is the circle, the segment and the point $(0, 1.5)$. A set with no width is all boundary.

screens.title: The same on the line
screens.question: Which statements are true? Select all that apply.

options.why: 0 is a boundary point but not in $A$. Boundary points need not belong to the set.
1 is in $A$, but every interval round 1 holds numbers above 1, outside $A$.

hints.text: Test 0, 1 and 2 one at a time.
2 is isolated: no interval round it lies in $A$.
Interior $(0, 1)$, closure adds 0, boundary is 0, 1 and 2.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Check each of 0, 1 and 2.

explain.text: $A^\circ = (0, 1)$ and $\overline{A} = [0, 1] \cup \{2\}$, so $\partial A = \{0, 1, 2\}$. The point 0 is on the boundary but not in $A$.

screens.title: A set full of holes
screens.prose: Take $\mathbb{Q}$, the rationals, inside $\mathbb{R}$. Every interval holds both rationals and irrationals.
screens.question: What are $\mathbb{Q}^\circ$, $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$ and $\partial \mathbb{Q}$?

options.why: You treated $\mathbb{Q}$ as open and closed. Every interval round a rational holds an irrational, so no point is interior.
$\sqrt2$ is a limit of rationals, so it is in the closure. The closure is all of $\mathbb{R}$.

hints.text: Can an interval fit inside $\mathbb{Q}$?
Every ball round $\sqrt2$ meets $\mathbb{Q}$.
Interior empty; closure everything; so the boundary is everything.

feedback.correct: Right. $\mathbb{Q}$ has no interior and is dense.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Every interval meets both $\mathbb{Q}$ and its complement.

explain.text: No interval lies inside $\mathbb{Q}$, so $\mathbb{Q}^\circ = \varnothing$. Every interval meets $\mathbb{Q}$, so $\overline{\mathbb{Q}} = \mathbb{R}$ and $\partial\mathbb{Q} = \mathbb{R} \setminus \varnothing = \mathbb{R}$.

screens.title: Outside the closure
screens.prose: We prove $(\overline{A})^c = (A^c)^\circ$ in any metric space. Each line is equivalent to the next.
screens.question: Put the chain in order. Move the flawed line to Left out.

lines.text: $x \in (\overline{A})^c$ means $x$ is not a closure point of $A$.
So some ball $B(x, r)$ does not meet $A$, by the definition of closure point.
So some ball $B(x, r)$ lies inside $A^c$, since missing $A$ means lying in $A^c$.
That says $x \in (A^c)^\circ$, by the definition of interior point. $\blacksquare$
So every ball $B(x, r)$ lies inside $A^c$.
lines.why: Negating "every ball meets $A$" gives "some ball misses $A$". Large balls round $x$ may still meet $A$.

hints.text: Negate "every ball meets $A$" carefully.
Not every ball meets $A$, so some ball misses it.

feedback.correct: Right. Closure and interior swap under complements.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Unpack each definition one step at a time.

byKey.d1: You negated "every" to "every". The negation of "every ball meets $A$" is "some ball misses $A$".
byKey.left-out: You left out a line the chain needs.

explain.text: Not a closure point means some ball misses $A$, that is, lies in $A^c$. That is exactly an interior point of $A^c$. So $(\overline{A})^c = (A^c)^\circ$.

screens.title: The smallest closed set
screens.prose: Use the last screen to show $\overline{A}$ is closed, and that it lies inside every closed $F \supseteq A$.
screens.question: Put the proof in order.

lines.text: An interior is open: a ball inside $A^c$ is open (l2), so each of its points is interior too.
So $(\overline{A})^c$ is open, and $\overline{A}$ is closed.
Now let $F \supseteq A$ be closed, and $x \notin F$. The open $F^c$ holds a ball round $x$.
That ball misses $F$, so it misses $A$, and $x \notin \overline{A}$. So $\overline{A} \subseteq F$. $\blacksquare$

hints.text: First closed, then smallest.
For smallest, show a point outside $F$ is outside $\overline{A}$.

feedback.correct: Right. $\overline{A}$ is the smallest closed set holding $A$.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Prove $\overline{A}$ closed first, then compare it with $F$.

explain.text: The complement of $\overline{A}$ is an interior, which is open, so $\overline{A}$ is closed. A point outside a closed $F \supseteq A$ has a ball missing $A$. So $\overline{A}$ sits inside every such $F$.

screens.title: Closure by sequences
screens.prose: `analysis` l23 proved closed sets contain their limits. Now we show $x \in \overline{A}$ exactly when some sequence in $A$ converges to $x$.
screens.question: Put both directions in order. Move the flawed line to Left out.

lines.text: Let $x \in \overline{A}$. Each ball $B(x, \tfrac1n)$ meets $A$; pick $a_n$ in it.
Then $d(a_n, x) < \tfrac1n \to 0$, so $a_n \to x$ with every $a_n \in A$.
Conversely let $a_n \in A$ with $a_n \to x$, and take any ball $B(x, r)$.
For $n$ large, $d(a_n, x) < r$, so the ball holds $a_n \in A$. Hence $x \in \overline{A}$. $\blacksquare$

lines.why: That needs $x \in A$. A rim point such as $(1, 0)$ for the open disc is in $\overline{A}$ but not in $A$.

hints.text: Shrink the balls as $\tfrac1n$.
Forward: one point per ball. Backward: the tail of the sequence enters any ball.

feedback.correct: Right. Closure points are exactly limits of points of $A$.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Prove the forward direction with balls of radius $\tfrac1n$.

byKey.d1: You used $x$ itself, which may not be in $A$. Pick $a_n$ from $A$ inside each ball.
byKey.left-out: You left out a line the proof needs.

explain.text: Picking $a_n \in A \cap B(x, \tfrac1n)$ gives a sequence in $A$ tending to $x$. Conversely a sequence in $A$ tending to $x$ enters every ball round $x$.

screens.title: Does the boundary belong?
screens.prose: Take $A = (0, 1]$ on the line. Three points are marked.
screens.question: Tap every boundary point of $A$.

hints.text: A boundary point need not be in $A$.
Every interval round 0 holds points of $A$.
Both ends: 0 and 1.

feedback.correct: Right. One boundary point inside $A$, one outside.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Test each point: does every interval round it meet $A$ and $A^c$?

byKey.b0: You missed 0. You took boundary points to belong to the set, but 0 is outside $A$ and still on its edge.
byKey.bh: 0.5 has the interval $(0.4, 0.6)$ inside $A$. It is interior.

explain.text: Every interval round 0 meets $A$ and its complement, and so does every interval round 1. So $\partial A = \{0, 1\}$. One end is in $A$ and one is not.

screens.title: A closed ball that is not the closure
screens.prose: In the discrete metric, $B(x, 1) = \{x\}$, while the closed ball $\{y : d(x, y) \le 1\}$ is all of $X$.
screens.question: Take $X$ with at least two points. What is the closure of $B(x, 1)$?

options.text: $\{x\}$, since every set is closed in the discrete metric

options.why: You took the closure of a ball to be the closed ball. Here $\{x\}$ is already closed, so it is its own closure.

options.text: $\{x\}$ together with the points at distance exactly 1
options.why: A point $y \ne x$ has $B(y, \tfrac12) = \{y\}$, which misses $\{x\}$. So $y$ is no closure point.

hints.text: Is $\{x\}$ closed? Its complement is a union of singletons.
A closed set is its own closure.

feedback.correct: Right. The closure is $\{x\}$; the closed ball is $X$.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Every set is open here, so every set is also closed.

explain.text: Every set is open in the discrete metric, so every complement is closed too. So $\overline{B(x, 1)} = \{x\} \ne X$. In a normed space such as $\mathbb{R}^n$ the two agree.

screens.title: Valid correlation matrices
screens.prose: Three assets share one correlation $\rho$. The matrix has eigenvalues $1 + 2\rho$ and $1 - \rho$ (twice). It is a valid correlation matrix when every eigenvalue is at least 0.
screens.question: What is the smallest valid $\rho$?

hints.text: $1 - \rho \ge 0$ holds for every $\rho \le 1$.
Solve $1 + 2\rho \ge 0$.

feedback.correct: Right. At $\rho = -0.5$ the eigenvalues are 0, 1.5 and 1.5.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Which eigenvalue turns negative first?

byKey.minus-one: Each pair may have correlation $-1$, but three assets cannot all move against each other. At $\rho = -1$, $1 + 2\rho = -1$.
byKey.three: You used $1 + 3\rho$. With three assets the top eigenvalue is $1 + 2\rho$.

explain.text: The valid set is $[-0.5, 1]$, and at $\rho = -0.5$ the eigenvalues are 0, 1.5 and 1.5. With $n$ assets the lower end is $-\tfrac{1}{n - 1}$, so $-\tfrac19 \approx -0.1111$ for 10.

screens.title: Where the inverse lives
screens.prose: A risk model inverts the correlation matrix. It is invertible exactly when no eigenvalue is 0. A stress test pushes $\rho$ towards 1.
screens.question: Which set of $\rho$ gives an invertible matrix, and what is it to the valid set?

options.text: $(-0.5, 1)$, the interior of the valid set $[-0.5, 1]$

options.why: At the ends an eigenvalue is 0, so the inverse fails there. The ends are the boundary.
You swapped the two. The boundary is exactly where an eigenvalue hits 0.

hints.text: Remove both ends from $[-0.5, 1]$.

feedback.correct: Right. The model lives in the interior; the stress test hits the boundary.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Find where an eigenvalue is exactly 0.

explain.text: Eigenvalues vanish only at $\rho = -0.5$ and $\rho = 1$, the boundary of $[-0.5, 1]$. So the invertible set is the interior $(-0.5, 1)$. A stress test pushing $\rho$ to 1 lands where the inverse fails.

ideas: $x$ is a closure point of $A$ when every ball round it meets $A$. It is interior when some ball lies inside $A$. The boundary is $\partial A = \overline{A} \setminus A^\circ$.
$(\overline{A})^c = (A^c)^\circ$, so $\overline{A}$ is closed, the smallest closed set holding $A$. It is the set of limits of sequences in $A$.
Boundary points need not lie in $A$: $\partial(0, 1] = \{0, 1\}$. In the discrete metric the closure of $B(x, 1)$ is $\{x\}$, not the closed ball $X$.

formula.name: Boundary
formula.note: Every ball round a boundary point meets both $A$ and $A^c$.

summary.trap: Boundary points need not belong to the set: 0 is on the boundary of $(0, 1]$ but not in it.

options.why: Each $\tfrac1n$ is in $A$ but has no interval inside $A$, so it is a boundary point too.
You left out 0. Every interval round 0 holds some $\tfrac1n$.

feedback.correct: Right. Interior empty, so the boundary is the closure.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Find the interior and the closure first.

quiz.prose: Let $A = \{(x, y) : 0 < x^2 + y^2 < 1\}$, the open disc without its centre.
quiz.question: What is $\partial A$?

options.text: The unit circle together with the origin

options.why: Every ball round the origin meets $A$ and also holds the origin, which is outside $A$.
Points with $0 < x^2 + y^2 < 1$ have a small ball inside $A$, so they are interior.

feedback.correct: Right. The missing centre is a boundary point.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Test the origin and a point on the circle.

explain.text: $A^\circ = A$ and $\overline{A}$ is the closed disc. So $\partial A$ is the circle plus the origin.

quiz.prose: Let $A$ be a subset of a metric space.
quiz.question: When is $A$ closed?

options.why: $[0, 1]$ is closed with boundary $\{0, 1\}$. An empty boundary means open and closed at once.
$[0, 1]$ is closed but its interior $(0, 1)$ is not boundary.

explain.text: $A$ is closed when $\overline{A} = A$, and $\overline{A} = A^\circ \cup \partial A$. Since $A^\circ \subseteq A$ always, this holds exactly when $\partial A \subseteq A$.
